query: Which method can be used for oxidation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Stationary friction processing (SFP) can be used to improve the oxidation resistance of AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi alloy with coarse grains (~98 μm) and nonprotective spinel oxide formation under high-temperature oxidation.
generation.intervention: Application of stationary friction processing at elevated rotational speeds (e.g., 1800 rpm) to induce an ultrafine‐grain microstructure.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in laboratory air at elevated temperatures (850–1050 °C) for prolonged durations (e.g., 100 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: Refined grain structure (grain size reduced to sub-micron levels, e.g., 0.43 μm) along with increased grain boundary density and elevated surface free energy.
generation.mechanism: The ultrafine grains and increased grain boundary density accelerate the outward diffusion of protective elements (like Cr and Al), facilitating the formation of dense, adherent protective oxide layers (Cr₂O₃ and Al₂O₃) while suppressing the formation of nonprotective spinel oxides.
generation.predicted_outcome: A deceleration in oxidation kinetics (i.e., lower cumulative mass gain and parabolic rate constants) compared to as-cast material, indicating enhanced high-temperature oxidation resistance.
generation.baseline: Coarse-grained as-cast samples show higher oxidation rates and formation of nonprotective spinel oxides such as Co(Cr,Fe)₂O₄.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected within the tested temperature range and specific alloy composition; its generality to other alloy systems or oxidation environments requires further study.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of oxidation resistance improvement and the influence of processing parameters need further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi alloy samples: one set as-cast (control) and another subjected to SFP at 1800 rpm. Expose both sets to isothermal oxidation tests at temperatures of 850 °C, 950 °C, and 1050 °C for 100 hours. Characterize the oxide scales and measure cumulative mass gain.
measurements: Oxide phase identification via XRD and SEM-EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SFP-processed samples do not exhibit a significantly lower mass gain and the formation of predominantly protective oxide phases (Cr₂O₃ and Al₂O₃) relative to the as-cast samples, then the hypothesis that SFP enhances oxidation resistance via microstructural refinement is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How does an ultrafine-grain microstructure, obtained via stationary friction processing, affect the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy?. System: Equimolar AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Stationary friction processing (SFP) using a WC-cylindrical tool (12 mm diameter) at rotational speeds of 400 rpm and 1800 rpm for 5 min duration. Test conditions: Isothermal oxidation in laboratory air at 850, 950, and 1050 °C for 100 h. Findings: Grain size refined from 98 μm (as-cast) to 1 μm (SFP_400) and 0.43 μm (SFP_1800).; Phase transformation from BCC/B2 to FCC occurred, with 38% and 55% FCC fraction for SFP_400 and SFP_1800, respectively.; Surface free energy increased by 29.8% for SFP_400 and 35.2% for SFP_1800 compared to as-cast.; Oxidation kinetics decelerated by 12–20% for SFP_400 and 38–48% for SFP_1800 compared to as-cast.; Cumulative mass gain at 850 °C after 100 h was 0.33 mg/cm² (as-cast), 0.27 mg/cm² (SFP_400), and 0.17 mg/cm² (SFP_1800).; Parabolic rate constants (k_p) at 1050 °C were 23.2 × 10⁻¹³ g²·cm⁻⁴·s⁻¹ (as-cast), 18.4 × 10⁻¹³ (SFP_400), and 8.16 × 10⁻¹³ (SFP_1800).; Processed samples formed predominantly protective
